1All the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron saying, “Look, we are your very flesh and blood! 2In the past, when Saul was our king, you were the real leader in Israel. The [[sc:Lord]] said to you, ‘You will shepherd my people Israel; you will rule over Israel.’”

3When all the leaders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, King David made an agreement with them in Hebron before the [[sc:Lord]]. They designated David as king over Israel. 4David was thirty years old when he began to reign and he reigned for forty years. 5In Hebron he reigned over Judah for seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned for thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.

6Then the king and his men advanced to Jerusalem against the Jebusites who lived in the land. The Jebusites said to David, “You cannot invade this place! Even the blind and the lame will turn you back, saying, ‘David cannot invade this place!’”

7But David captured the fortress of Zion (that is, the City of David). 8David said on that day, “Whoever attacks the Jebusites must approach the ‘lame’ and the ‘blind’ who are David’s enemies by going through the water tunnel.” For this reason it is said, “The blind and the lame cannot enter the palace.”

9So David lived in the fortress and called it the City of David. David built all around it, from the terrace inwards. 10David’s power grew steadily, for the [[sc:Lord]] God of Heaven’s Armies was with him.

11King Hiram of Tyre sent messengers to David, along with cedar logs, carpenters, and stonemasons. They built a palace for David. 12David realized that the [[sc:Lord]] had established him as king over Israel and that he had elevated his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel. 13David married more concubines and wives from Jerusalem after he arrived from Hebron. Even more sons and daughters were born to David. 14These are the names of children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, 15Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia, 16Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.

17When the Philistines heard that David had been designated king over Israel, they all went up to search for David. When David heard about it, he went down to the fortress. 18Now the Philistines had arrived and spread out in the valley of Rephaim. 19So David asked the [[sc:Lord]], “Should I march up against the Philistines? Will you hand them over to me?” The [[sc:Lord]] said to David, “March up, for I will indeed hand the Philistines over to you.”

20So David marched against Baal Perazim and defeated them there. Then he said, “The [[sc:Lord]] has burst out against my enemies like water bursts out.” So he called the name of that place Baal Perazim. 21The Philistines abandoned their idols there, and David and his men picked them up.

22The Philistines again came up and spread out in the valley of Rephaim. 23So David asked the [[sc:Lord]] what he should do. This time the [[sc:Lord]] said to him, “Don’t march straight up. Instead, circle around behind them and come against them opposite the trees. 24When you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the trees, act decisively. For at that moment the [[sc:Lord]] is going before you to strike down the army of the Philistines.” 25David did just as the [[sc:Lord]] commanded him, and he struck down the Philistines from Gibeon all the way to Gezer.

6:1David again assembled all the best men in Israel, 30,000 in number. 2David and all the men who were with him traveled to Baalah in Judah to bring up from there the ark of God which is called by the name of the [[sc:Lord]] of Heaven’s Armies, who sits enthroned between the cherubim that are on it. 3They loaded the ark of God on a new cart and carried it from the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill. Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were guiding the new cart. 4They brought it with the ark of God from the house of Abinadab on the hill. Ahio was walking in front of the ark, 5while David and all Israel were energetically celebrating before the [[sc:Lord]], singing and playing various stringed instruments, tambourines, rattles, and cymbals.

6When they arrived at the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah reached out and grabbed hold of the ark of God, because the oxen stumbled. 7The [[sc:Lord]] was so furious with Uzzah, he killed him on the spot for his negligence. He died right there beside the ark of God.

8David was angry because the [[sc:Lord]] attacked Uzzah; so he called that place Perez Uzzah, which remains its name to this very day. 9David was afraid of the [[sc:Lord]] that day and said, “How will the ark of the [[sc:Lord]] ever come to me?” 10So David was no longer willing to bring the ark of the [[sc:Lord]] to be with him in the City of David. David left it in the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite. 11The ark of the [[sc:Lord]] remained in the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite for three months. The [[sc:Lord]] blessed Obed-Edom and all his family. 12King David was told, “The [[sc:Lord]] has blessed the family of Obed-Edom and everything he owns because of the ark of God.” So David went and joyfully brought the ark of God from the house of Obed-Edom to the City of David. 13Those who carried the ark of the [[sc:Lord]] took six steps and then David sacrificed an ox and a fatling calf. 14Now David, wearing a linen ephod, was dancing with all his strength before the [[sc:Lord]]. 15David and all Israel were bringing up the ark of the [[sc:Lord]], shouting and blowing trumpets.

16As the ark of the [[sc:Lord]] entered the City of David, Saul’s daughter Michal looked out the window. When she saw King David leaping and dancing before the [[sc:Lord]], she despised him. 17They brought the ark of the [[sc:Lord]] and put it in its place in the middle of the tent that David had pitched for it. Then David offered burnt sacrifices and peace offerings before the [[sc:Lord]]. 18When David finished offering the burnt sacrifices and peace offerings, he pronounced a blessing over the people in the name of the [[sc:Lord]] of Heaven’s Armies. 19He then handed out to each member of the entire assembly of Israel, both men and women, a portion of bread, a date cake, and a raisin cake. Then all the people went home. 20When David went home to pronounce a blessing on his own house, Michal, Saul’s daughter, came out to meet him. She said, “How the king of Israel has distinguished himself this day! He has exposed himself today before his servants’ slave girls the way a vulgar fool might do!”

21David replied to Michal, “It was before the [[sc:Lord]]! I was celebrating before the [[sc:Lord]], who chose me over your father and his entire family and appointed me as leader over the [[sc:Lord]]’s people Israel. 22I am willing to shame and humiliate myself even more than this. But with the slave girls whom you mentioned, let me be distinguished.” 23Now Michal, Saul’s daughter, had no children to the day of her death.

elements.question: Tap to see what ‘Messiah’ means.
elements.answer: ‘Messiah’ is a Hebrew word meaning ‘anointed one’. (Its Greek equivalent is ‘Christ’.) Kings in Israel were anointed with oil to show that God had set them apart for the task. As the story goes on, ‘the Messiah’ comes to mean the ideal king whom God promised to send. The New Testament study shows who that is.

elements.text: A house for God?

elements.passageText:
1The king settled into his palace, for the [[sc:Lord]] gave him relief from all his enemies on all sides. 2The king said to Nathan the prophet, “Look! I am living in a palace made from cedar, while the ark of God sits in the middle of a tent.” 3Nathan replied to the king, “You should go and do whatever you have in mind, for the [[sc:Lord]] is with you.”

4That night the [[sc:Lord]]’s message came to Nathan, 5“Go, tell my servant David, ‘This is what the [[sc:Lord]] has said: Do you really intend to build a house for me to live in? 6I have not lived in a house from the time I brought the Israelites up from Egypt to the present day. Instead, I was traveling with them and living in a tent. 7Wherever I moved among all the Israelites, I did not say to any of their leaders whom I appointed to care for my people Israel, “Why have you not built me a house made from cedar?”’

8“So now, say this to my servant David, ‘This is what the [[sc:Lord]] of Heaven’s Armies has said: I took you from the pasture and from your work as a shepherd to make you leader of my people Israel. 9I was with you wherever you went, and I defeated all your enemies before you. Now I will make you as famous as the great men of the earth. 10I will establish a place for my people Israel and settle them there; they will live there and not be disturbed anymore. Violent men will not oppress them again, as they did in the beginning 11and during the time when I appointed judges to lead my people Israel. Instead, I will give you relief from all your enemies. The [[sc:Lord]] declares to you that he himself will build a dynastic house for you. 12When the time comes for you to die, I will raise up your descendant, one of your own sons, to succeed you, and I will establish his kingdom. 13He will build a house for my name, and I will make his dynasty permanent. 14I will become his father and he will become my son. When he sins, I will correct him with the rod of men and with wounds inflicted by human beings. 15But my loyal love will not be removed from him as I removed it from Saul, whom I removed from before you. 16Your house and your kingdom will stand before me permanently; your dynasty will be permanent.’” 17Nathan told David all these words that were revealed to him.

elements.question: What does David want to do for God, and how does God respond in verses 4–7?
elements.questionHint: Notice the difference between David’s own house and the place where God’s ark has been.
elements.sampleAnswer: David has a fine palace of cedar, yet God’s ark still sits in a tent. He proposes to build God a temple, and the prophet Nathan initially says to go ahead. That night God corrects him: he has never asked for any such building, and has always travelled with his people in a tent. God has no need of David’s construction project.
elements.mainPoint: **God does not need our building for him**: he is the one who provides.

elements.question: What has God already done for David, and what does he promise to do for Israel in verses 8–11?
elements.questionHint: Look at the verbs after ‘I’ in verses 8–11.
elements.sampleAnswer: God reminds David that he began as a shepherd. God made him leader of Israel, stayed by his side and defeated his rivals. He will make David famous, on a par with the most celebrated people in history. For Israel, he will provide a safe homeland where they can settle, free from their enemies.
elements.mainPoint: God has **raised David from shepherd to ruler**, and will give Israel a secure place and rest.

elements.question: In verses 11–16 God says he will build a ‘house’ for David. What does he mean, and what will last for ever?
elements.questionHint: Notice who is building whose house in verses 11–13.
elements.sampleAnswer: God turns David’s offer round: David will not be building God a house, but God will build one for David, meaning a royal dynasty. A son of David will take over and God will secure his kingdom. That son will construct a temple for God’s name, and his royal line is promised to endure permanently. The relationship is that of a father and son: discipline for wrongdoing, but never the withdrawal of love.
elements.mainPoint: God will **build David a house**: a son whose kingdom is permanent, whom God will father and discipline but never abandon.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: David’s son Solomon built the temple, but his kingdom did not last. What might that suggest about whether this promise has been fully fulfilled?

elements.question: Which parts of the pattern from Eden (people, place and rule) can you find in verses 8–16?
elements.questionHint: Look for a people, a place and a king.
elements.sampleAnswer: People: God promises Israel peace and safety instead of oppression. Place: God will give them a home of their own, in which no one will disturb them. Rule: a king from David’s family whose royal line and realm are guaranteed permanently. Together, these restore the Eden pattern of a people with a place under a ruler.
elements.mainPoint: The promise **brings the kingdom pattern together again**: **God’s people** (Israel, settled), **God’s place** (the land) and **God’s rule** (a king from David’s line).

elements.text: David’s prayer

elements.passageText:
18King David went in, sat before the [[sc:Lord]], and said, “Who am I, O Sovereign [[sc:Lord]], and what is my family, that you should have brought me to this point? 19And you didn’t stop there, O [[sc:Lord]] God! You have also spoken about the future of your servant’s family. Is this your usual way of dealing with men, O Sovereign [[sc:Lord]]? 20What more can David say to you? You have given your servant special recognition, O Sovereign [[sc:Lord]]! 21For the sake of your promise and according to your purpose you have done this great thing in order to reveal it to your servant. 22Therefore you are great, O Sovereign [[sc:Lord]], for there is none like you. There is no God besides you! What we have heard is true. 23Who is like your people, Israel, a unique nation on the earth? Their God went to claim a nation for himself and to make a name for himself! You did great and awesome acts for your land, before your people whom you delivered for yourself from the Egyptian empire and its gods. 24You made Israel your very own people for all time. You, O [[sc:Lord]], became their God.

25So now, O [[sc:Lord]] God, make this promise you have made about your servant and his family a permanent reality. Do as you promised, 26so you may gain lasting fame, as people say, ‘The [[sc:Lord]] of Heaven’s Armies is God over Israel!’ The dynasty of your servant David will be established before you, 27for you, O [[sc:Lord]] of Heaven’s Armies, the God of Israel, have told your servant, ‘I will build you a dynastic house.’ That is why your servant has had the courage to pray this prayer to you. 28Now, O Sovereign [[sc:Lord]], you are the true God. May your words prove to be true! You have made this good promise to your servant. 29Now be willing to bless your servant’s dynasty so that it may stand permanently before you, for you, O Sovereign [[sc:Lord]], have spoken. By your blessing may your servant’s dynasty be blessed from now on into the future!”

elements.question: How does David see himself in front of God in verses 18–24, and what does he say about God and Israel?
elements.questionHint: Notice how David speaks of himself and of his house.
elements.sampleAnswer: David is humbled that the Lord has done so much for someone like him. He asks who he is and what his family is to deserve this, and keeps calling himself God’s servant. He praises God as incomparable: there is no one like him and no other God. And he marvels that God rescued Israel from Egypt to be his own people.
elements.mainPoint: David is **humbled** that the incomparable God has chosen and honoured him.

elements.question: What does David ask God to do in verses 25–29, and why?
elements.questionHint: Look for what David asks God to keep and confirm.
elements.sampleAnswer: David wants God to follow through on what he has said: the promise concerning David’s family must stay in force permanently. His aim is God’s fame, so that people everywhere declare that the Lord rules over Israel. He therefore pleads for blessing on his royal line so that it stands for ever. He can ask this boldly because the promise came from God himself, who is faithful.
elements.mainPoint: David **prays for God to keep his promise**, for the sake of God’s own fame.

elements.text: Reflect

elements.question: David wanted to do something for God, but God told him he would do something for David. How does that challenge the way you think about serving God?
God promises a king whose kingdom will last for ever, yet every earthly ruler falls short. Where do you see the need for a better king today? How does that shape your prayers?

elements.text:
Now the three parts of the kingdom are in view again: a people, a place and a king. But kings die, and David’s own family falls short. The promise of a king who rules for ever is a promise still waiting to be kept. Next session we see what happens when the kingdom falls apart.

Now tap Read more below to go deeper.
Where we are in the story: Israel had a king and a land, but both are lost. In exile, God makes a promise that goes to the root of the problem.

elements.question: Has anyone ever given you a second chance? What did it feel like, and what did it cost them?

elements.text:
Since last time: David’s son Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem, and Israel reached its high point. After Solomon the kingdom split in two: Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Most of the kings turned away from God and the people followed idols. God sent prophets such as Elijah, Isaiah and Jeremiah to call the people back, and warned that if they did not repent they would lose the land. The northern kingdom fell to Assyria. In 586 BC Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, and took many of the people into exile.

All three parts of the kingdom were lost: the people were scattered, the land was taken and the king was gone. Jeremiah spoke of the judgement. He also spoke of hope.

elements.question: Tap to see what to read.
elements.answer:
Read 2 Kings 25:1–21 (the fall of Jerusalem) and Jeremiah 29:1–14 (Jeremiah’s letter to the exiles, with God’s promise of a future).

2 Kings 25:1–21 (NET)

1So King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon came against Jerusalem with his whole army and set up camp outside it. They built siege ramps all around it. He arrived on the tenth day of the tenth month in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign. 2The city remained under siege until King Zedekiah’s eleventh year. 3By the ninth day of the fourth month the famine in the city was so severe the residents had no food. 4The enemy broke through the city walls, and all the soldiers tried to escape. They left the city during the night. They went through the gate between the two walls, which is near the king’s garden. (The Babylonians were all around the city.) Then they headed for the rift valley. 5But the Babylonian army chased after the king. They caught up with him in the rift valley plains of Jericho, and his entire army deserted him. 6They captured the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where he passed sentence on him. 7Zedekiah’s sons were executed while Zedekiah was forced to watch. The king of Babylon then had Zedekiah’s eyes put out, bound him in bronze chains, and carried him off to Babylon.

8On the seventh day of the fifth month, in the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, Nebuzaradan, the captain of the royal guard, who served the king of Babylon, arrived in Jerusalem. 9He burned down the [[sc:Lord]]’s temple, the royal palace, and all the houses in Jerusalem, including every large house. 10The whole Babylonian army that came with the captain of the royal guard tore down the walls that surrounded Jerusalem. 11Nebuzaradan, the captain of the royal guard, deported the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the craftsmen. 12But he left behind some of the poor of the land and gave them fields and vineyards.

13The Babylonians broke the two bronze pillars in the [[sc:Lord]]’s temple, as well as the movable stands and the big bronze basin called “The Sea.” They took the bronze to Babylon. 14They also took the pots, shovels, trimming shears, pans, and all the bronze utensils used by the priests. 15The captain of the royal guard took the golden and silver censers and basins. 16The bronze of the items that King Solomon made for the [[sc:Lord]]’s temple—including the two pillars, the big bronze basin called “The Sea,” the twelve bronze bulls under “The Sea,” and the movable stands—was too heavy to be weighed. 17Each of the pillars was about twenty-seven feet high. The bronze top of one pillar was about 4½ feet high and had bronze latticework and pomegranate-shaped ornaments all around it. The second pillar with its latticework was like it.

18The captain of the royal guard took Seraiah, the chief priest, and Zephaniah, the priest who was second in rank, and the three doorkeepers. 19From the city he took a eunuch who was in charge of the soldiers, five of the king’s advisers who were discovered in the city, an official army secretary who drafted citizens for military service, and sixty citizens from the people of the land who were discovered in the city. 20Nebuzaradan, captain of the royal guard, took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah. 21The king of Babylon ordered them to be executed at Riblah in the territory of Hamath. So Judah was deported from its land.

Jeremiah 29:1–14 (NET)

1The prophet Jeremiah sent a letter to the exiles Nebuchadnezzar had carried off from Jerusalem to Babylon. It was addressed to the elders who were left among the exiles, to the priests, to the prophets, and to all the other people who were exiled in Babylon. 2He sent it after King Jeconiah, the queen mother, the palace officials, the leaders of Judah and Jerusalem, the craftsmen, and the metal workers had been exiled from Jerusalem. 3He sent it with Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah. King Zedekiah of Judah had sent these men to Babylon to King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. The letter said:

4“The [[sc:Lord]] of Heaven’s Armies, the God of Israel, says to all those he sent into exile to Babylon from Jerusalem, 5‘Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat what they produce. 6Marry and have sons and daughters. Find wives for your sons and allow your daughters to get married so that they too can have sons and daughters. Grow in number; do not dwindle away. 7Work to see that the city where I sent you as exiles enjoys peace and prosperity. Pray to the [[sc:Lord]] for it. For as it prospers you will prosper.’

8“For the [[sc:Lord]] of Heaven’s Armies, the God of Israel, says, ‘Do not let the prophets among you or those who claim to be able to predict the future by divination deceive you. And do not pay any attention to the dreams that you are encouraging them to dream. 9They are prophesying lies to you and claiming my authority to do so. But I did not send them. I, the [[sc:Lord]], affirm it!’

10“For the [[sc:Lord]] says, ‘Only when the seventy years of Babylonian rule are over will I again take up consideration for you. Then I will fulfill my gracious promise to you and restore you to your homeland. 11For I know what I have planned for you,’ says the [[sc:Lord]]. ‘I have plans to prosper you, not to harm you. I have plans to give you a future filled with hope. 12When you call out to me and come to me in prayer, I will hear your prayers. 13When you seek me in prayer and worship, you will find me available to you. If you seek me with all your heart and soul, 14I will make myself available to you,’ says the [[sc:Lord]]. ‘Then I will reverse your plight and will regather you from all the nations and all the places where I have exiled you,’ says the [[sc:Lord]]. ‘I will bring you back to the place from which I exiled you.’

elements.text: A new covenant

elements.passageText: 31“Indeed, a time is coming,” says the [[sc:Lord]], “when I will make a new covenant with the people of Israel and Judah. 32It will not be like the old covenant that I made with their ancestors when I delivered them from Egypt. For they violated that covenant, even though I was like a faithful husband to them,” says the [[sc:Lord]]. 33“But I will make a new covenant with the whole nation of Israel after I plant them back in the land,” says the [[sc:Lord]]. “I will put my law within them and write it on their hearts and minds. I will be their God and they will be my people. 34“People will no longer need to teach their neighbors and relatives to know me. For all of them, from the least important to the most important, will know me,” says the [[sc:Lord]]. “For I will forgive their sin and will no longer call to mind the wrong they have done.”

elements.question: Who will God make this new covenant with, and when (verse 31)?
elements.questionHint: Look at the words ‘a time is coming’ and the two names given.
elements.sampleAnswer: God says a time is coming when he will make a new covenant with the people of Israel and Judah, the two parts of the divided kingdom. So the promise looks beyond the present disaster to a future time when God will act. It is addressed to the same people who have been in exile, so the broken people will have a fresh start.
elements.mainPoint: God promises **a new covenant** for his people, looking beyond the exile to a time when he will act.
keyTerms: a time is coming|days are coming|futur|time

elements.question: How does God describe the old covenant, and what went wrong with it (verse 32)?
elements.questionHint: Notice who broke the covenant, and what God says about his own part.
elements.sampleAnswer: The old covenant was the agreement made with Israel’s ancestors when God rescued them from Egypt. God likens himself to a faithful husband. Yet the people violated it, so the fault lay with them rather than with him. This explains why a fresh start is needed.
elements.mainPoint: The old covenant failed because **the people broke it**, not because God did.

elements.question: What will be different about the new covenant (verse 33)?
elements.questionHint: Think about where the law will be.
elements.sampleAnswer: Under the new arrangement the problem of outward rules is solved from within: God himself puts his instruction inside his people and engraves it on their hearts and minds. He renews the old relationship, so he is their God and they are his people. The transformation originates with him, not with human effort.
elements.mainPoint: In the new covenant **God changes hearts**: his law is written inside his people, and they are truly his.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: At Sinai (session 4) God’s law was given to a people gathered at the foot of a mountain. How does this picture of the law on the heart compare?

elements.question: What does verse 34 promise about knowing God, and about sin?
elements.questionHint: Look at who knows God, and what God says he will do with their sins.
elements.sampleAnswer: Everyone under this covenant will know the Lord personally, from the least important to the most important. So nobody will need to teach a neighbour to know him. Behind this is God’s promise to forgive their sin. He will no longer call to mind the wrong they have done. Forgiveness is what makes knowing him possible.
elements.mainPoint: In the new covenant **everyone knows God**, because their sin is forgiven.

elements.question: The covenant is called ‘new’. In what ways is it new, and in what ways does God’s purpose stay the same?
elements.questionHint: Compare verse 33, ‘I will be their God and they will be my people’, with what is new.
elements.sampleAnswer: It is new because the law will be inside the people, everyone will know the Lord and sins will be forgiven. But the purpose is the same: God will be their God and they will be his people, the relationship God has always intended. The covenant is renewed, not abandoned, and the same God keeps the same purpose.
elements.mainPoint: The new covenant is **new in power but the same in purpose**: God and his people together.

elements.question: Jeremiah’s promise is that God will change people from the inside. Where do you find that your own heart needs changing, rather than just your behaviour?
The people were in exile when they heard this promise. How can a promise about the future help someone who is in a hard place now?

elements.text:
Jeremiah’s promise reaches the root of the problem: not a better set of rules but a changed heart, and a forgiveness that makes it possible to know God. But the passage does not say how sin will be dealt with. The next session looks at a prophet who does.

Where we are in the story: God has promised a new covenant with forgiveness of sin. But how can sin be forgiven? This session we read the Old Testament’s most searching answer.

elements.question: Think of a time when someone suffered on behalf of someone else. What did it do for the other person?

elements.text:
Since last time: After many years in exile, Persia’s King Cyrus allowed the Jews to return. They rebuilt the temple and later the walls of Jerusalem, as Ezra and Nehemiah describe. But it was not the glorious restoration the prophets had promised. The people were back in the land, but under foreign rule, and there was no king from David’s line.

The prophet Isaiah had spoken long before about a servant of the Lord who would bring the true restoration. His fourth song of the servant, in Isaiah 52–53, is the passage for this session.

elements.question: Tap to see what to read.
elements.answer:
Read Ezra 1 (the return from exile), Isaiah 40:1–11 (comfort for God’s people) and Isaiah 42:1–9 (the first song of the servant).

Ezra 1 (NET)

1In the first year of King Cyrus of Persia, in fulfillment of the [[sc:Lord]]’s message spoken through Jeremiah, the [[sc:Lord]] motivated King Cyrus of Persia to issue a proclamation throughout his kingdom and also to put it in writing. It read:

2“This is what King Cyrus of Persia says: “‘The [[sc:Lord]] God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth. He has appointed me to build a temple for him in Jerusalem, which is in Judah.

3Anyone of his people among you (may his God be with him!) may go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and may build the temple of the [[sc:Lord]] God of Israel—he is the God who is in Jerusalem. 4Anyone who survives in any of those places where he is a resident foreigner must be helped by his neighbors with silver, gold, equipment, and animals, along with voluntary offerings for the temple of God which is in Jerusalem.’”

5Then the leaders of Judah and Benjamin, along with the priests and the Levites—all those whose mind God had stirred—got ready to go up in order to build the temple of the [[sc:Lord]] in Jerusalem. 6All their neighbors assisted them with silver utensils, gold, equipment, animals, and expensive gifts, not to mention all the voluntary offerings.

7Then King Cyrus brought out the vessels of the [[sc:Lord]]’s temple which Nebuchadnezzar had brought from Jerusalem and had displayed in the temple of his gods. 8King Cyrus of Persia entrusted them to Mithredath the treasurer, who counted them out to Sheshbazzar the leader of the Judahite exiles.

9The inventory of these items was as follows: 30 gold basins, 1,000 silver basins, 29 silver utensils, 1030 gold bowls, 410 other silver bowls, and 1,000 other vessels.

11All these gold and silver vessels totaled 5,400. Sheshbazzar brought them all along when the captives were brought up from Babylon to Jerusalem.

Isaiah 40:1–11 (NET)

1“Comfort, comfort my people,” says your God. 2“Speak kindly to Jerusalem and tell her that her time of warfare is over, that her punishment is completed. For the [[sc:Lord]] has made her pay double for all her sins.” 3A voice cries out, “In the wilderness clear a way for the [[sc:Lord]]; build a level road through the rift valley for our God. 4Every valley must be elevated, and every mountain and hill leveled. The rough terrain will become a level plain, the rugged landscape a wide valley. 5The splendor of the [[sc:Lord]] will be revealed, and all people will see it at the same time. For the [[sc:Lord]] has decreed it.” 6A voice says, “Cry out!” Another asks, “What should I cry out?” The first voice responds: “All people are like grass, and all their promises are like the flowers in the field. 7The grass dries up, the flowers wither, when the wind sent by the [[sc:Lord]] blows on them. Surely humanity is like grass. 8The grass dries up, the flowers wither, but the decree of our God is forever reliable.”

9Go up on a high mountain, O herald Zion. Shout out loudly, O herald Jerusalem! Shout, don’t be afraid! Say to the towns of Judah, “Here is your God!” 10Look, the Sovereign [[sc:Lord]] comes as a victorious warrior; his military power establishes his rule. Look, his reward is with him; his prize goes before him. 11Like a shepherd he tends his flock; he gathers up the lambs with his arm; he carries them close to his heart; he leads the ewes along.

Isaiah 42:1–9 (NET)

1“Here is my servant whom I support, my chosen one in whom I take pleasure. I have placed my Spirit on him; he will make just decrees for the nations. 2He will not cry out or shout; he will not publicize himself in the streets. 3A crushed reed he will not break, a dim wick he will not extinguish; he will faithfully make just decrees. 4He will not grow dim or be crushed before establishing justice on the earth; the coastlands will wait in anticipation for his decrees.” 5This is what the true God, the [[sc:Lord]], says— the one who created the sky and stretched it out, the one who fashioned the earth and everything that lives on it, the one who gives breath to the people on it, and life to those who live on it: 6“I, the [[sc:Lord]], officially commission you; I take hold of your hand. I protect you and make you a covenant mediator for people, and a light to the nations, 7to open blind eyes, to release prisoners from dungeons, those who live in darkness from prisons.

8“I am the [[sc:Lord]]! That is my name! I will not share my glory with anyone else, or the praise due me with idols. 9Look, my earlier predictive oracles have come to pass; now I announce new events. Before they begin to occur, I reveal them to you.”

elements.text: The servant of the Lord

elements.passageText:
13Look, my servant will succeed! He will be elevated, lifted high, and greatly exalted — 14(just as many were horrified by the sight of you) he was so disfigured he no longer looked like a man; his form was so marred he no longer looked human — 15so now he will startle many nations. Kings will be shocked by his exaltation, for they will witness something unannounced to them, and they will understand something they had not heard about.

53:1Who would have believed what we just heard? When was the [[sc:Lord]]’s power revealed through him? 2He sprouted up like a twig before God, like a root out of parched soil; he had no stately form or majesty that might catch our attention, no special appearance that we should want to follow him. 3He was despised and rejected by people, one who experienced pain and was acquainted with illness; people hid their faces from him; he was despised, and we considered him insignificant.

4But he lifted up our illnesses, he carried our pain; even though we thought he was being punished, attacked by God, and afflicted for something he had done. 5He was wounded because of our rebellious deeds, crushed because of our sins; he endured punishment that made us well; because of his wounds we have been healed. 6All of us had wandered off like sheep; each of us had strayed off on his own path, but the [[sc:Lord]] caused the sin of all of us to attack him.

7He was treated harshly and afflicted, but he did not even open his mouth. Like a lamb led to the slaughtering block, like a sheep silent before her shearers, he did not even open his mouth. 8He was led away after an unjust trial — but who even cared? Indeed, he was cut off from the land of the living; because of the rebellion of his own people he was wounded. 9They intended to bury him with criminals, but he ended up in a rich man’s tomb, because he had committed no violent deeds, nor had he spoken deceitfully.

10Though the [[sc:Lord]] desired to crush him and make him ill, once restitution is made, he will see descendants and enjoy long life, and the [[sc:Lord]]’s purpose will be accomplished through him. 11Having suffered, he will reflect on his work, he will be satisfied when he understands what he has done. “My servant will acquit many, for he carried their sins. 12So I will assign him a portion with the multitudes, he will divide the spoils of victory with the powerful, because he willingly submitted to death and was numbered with the rebels, when he lifted up the sin of many and intervened on behalf of the rebels.”

elements.question: How is the servant introduced in 52:13–15, and what surprises the nations and their kings?
elements.questionHint: Look for the contrast between ‘lifted up’ and ‘disfigured’.
elements.sampleAnswer: The servant is presented as someone who will succeed and be raised to the highest honour. Yet he is introduced through a shocking image: many people recoiled because his appearance was so disfigured that he looked scarcely human. What astonishes the nations is that kings will fall silent before him, seeing something none of them had been told. The surprise is that honour comes through suffering.
elements.mainPoint: The servant will be **raised to glory by way of suffering**, to the astonishment of nations and kings.

elements.question: How do people treat the servant in 53:1–3, and why?
elements.questionHint: Notice what the servant lacks in verse 2 and what people do with their faces in verse 3.
elements.sampleAnswer: He had nothing in his looks that would draw a crowd: no majesty and no striking appearance. Instead he was despised and rejected, familiar with pain and sickness. People turned their faces away, and he counted for nothing in their eyes. He was nothing like the powerful deliverer they would have hoped for.
elements.mainPoint: The servant is **despised and rejected**, not the kind of deliverer people expected.

elements.question: Whose sins and sufferings does the servant carry, according to 53:4–6? Look at how often ‘we’ and ‘our’ appear.
elements.questionHint: Count the ‘we’ and ‘our’, and notice who is described as wounded.
elements.sampleAnswer: In these verses the people speaking admit that the servant took their own burdens on himself. They once assumed he was being punished for something he himself had done, but he was wounded and crushed for their rebellion and sins. His suffering is what made them well. Like straying sheep, they had each gone their own way, and God directed the guilt of everyone onto him.
elements.mainPoint: The servant **suffers in the place of others**, bearing their sins so that they are healed.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Isaiah does not name the servant in these verses. Who do you think the first readers might have thought of?

elements.question: How does the servant face his suffering and death in 53:7–9?
elements.questionHint: Notice his response when he is oppressed, and what is said about his innocence.
elements.sampleAnswer: Faced with cruelty, the servant stays silent, as a lamb is when taken to be killed or as a sheep is before those who cut its wool. A trial rigged against him ends in his death. His enemies planned a criminal’s grave for him, yet he was laid in a wealthy man’s tomb, innocent as he was, having done no violence.
elements.mainPoint: The servant **bears injustice silently** and innocently, going to death like a lamb.
keyTerms: silent|quiet|did not even open|open his mouth|his mouth

elements.question: What does the Lord achieve through the servant’s suffering (53:10–12)? What happens to the servant afterwards?
elements.questionHint: Look at what the many receive, and at what the servant sees at the end.
elements.sampleAnswer: God’s plan was that his servant would suffer; yet once the guilt is dealt with, the servant will have many heirs and a long life, and the Lord’s purposes will succeed through him. After his anguish he will look at the outcome and be content. Because he bore the guilt of others, he will bring acquittal to many. He did this by willingly giving himself up to death among sinners and pleading for them.
elements.mainPoint: Through the servant’s suffering the Lord **acquits many**, and the servant is vindicated.

elements.text: Reflect

elements.question: Read verses 4–6 slowly, as if they were a prayer. What do you want to say to God in response?
In this passage God achieves his purpose through weakness, suffering and apparent failure. How does that challenge what we usually think of as success and strength?

elements.text:
The servant is the answer to the question left by Jeremiah’s new covenant. Sin will be forgiven because someone bears it. The servant is not named, and the Old Testament leaves him as a figure still waiting to be revealed. Next session we look at the hope that kept God’s people going through the long years of waiting.

Now tap Read more below to go deeper.
Where we are in the story: The Old Testament ends with a people back in the land, but still waiting. In this last session we look at the hope that kept them going.

elements.question: When you think about the future of the world, what do you hope for? What do you fear?

elements.text:
Since last time: After the return from exile, the prophets Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi called the people to rebuild, to trust God and to wait for his coming. Then the Old Testament falls silent. For roughly four hundred years the Jews lived under Persian, Greek and then Roman rule, with no king and no prophets. Their question was: when will God keep his promises?

Two passages show what they were hoping for. Daniel, who served under foreign rulers during the exile, saw a vision of a kingdom given to one like a son of man. Isaiah spoke of a new heavens and a new earth.

elements.question: Tap to see what to read.
elements.answer:
Read Ezra 3 (rebuilding the temple), Nehemiah 8 (the people hear God’s law) and Malachi 3:1–6 (a promise that God will come). For more, read Daniel 1–6 to see how God’s people lived under foreign rulers.

Ezra 3 (NET)

1When the seventh month arrived and the Israelites were living in their towns, the people assembled in Jerusalem. 2Then Jeshua the son of Jozadak and his priestly colleagues and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and his colleagues started to build the altar of the God of Israel so they could offer burnt offerings on it as required by the law of Moses the man of God. 3They established the altar on its foundations, even though they were in terror of the local peoples, and they offered burnt offerings on it to the [[sc:Lord]], both the morning and the evening offerings. 4They observed the Feast of Shelters as required and offered the proper number of daily burnt offerings according to the requirement for each day. 5Afterward they offered the continual burnt offerings and those for the new moons and those for all the holy assemblies of the [[sc:Lord]] and all those that were being voluntarily offered to the [[sc:Lord]]. 6From the first day of the seventh month they began to offer burnt offerings to the [[sc:Lord]]. However, the [[sc:Lord]]’s temple was not at that time established.

7So they provided money for the masons and carpenters, and food, beverages, and olive oil for the people of Sidon and Tyre, so that they would bring cedar timber from Lebanon to the seaport at Joppa, in accord with the edict of King Cyrus of Persia. 8In the second year after they had come to the temple of God in Jerusalem, in the second month, Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak initiated the work, along with the rest of their associates, the priests and the Levites, and all those who were coming to Jerusalem from the exile. They appointed the Levites who were at least twenty years old to take charge of the work on the [[sc:Lord]]’s temple. 9So Jeshua appointed both his sons and his relatives, Kadmiel and his sons (the sons of Yehudah), to take charge of the workers in the temple of God, along with the sons of Henadad, their sons, and their relatives the Levites. 10When the builders established the [[sc:Lord]]’s temple, the priests, ceremonially attired and with their clarions, and the Levites (the sons of Asaph) with their cymbals, stood to praise the [[sc:Lord]] according to the instructions left by King David of Israel. 11With antiphonal response they sang, praising and glorifying the [[sc:Lord]]: “For he is good; his loyal love toward Israel is forever.” All the people gave a loud shout as they praised the [[sc:Lord]] when the temple of the [[sc:Lord]] was established.

12Many of the priests, the Levites, and the leaders —older people who had seen with their own eyes the former temple while it was still established —were weeping loudly, and many others raised their voice in a joyous shout. 13People were unable to tell the difference between the sound of joyous shouting and the sound of the people’s weeping, for the people were shouting so loudly that the sound was heard a long way off.

Nehemiah 8 (NET)

1all the people gathered together in the plaza which was in front of the Water Gate. They asked Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses which the [[sc:Lord]] had commanded Israel. 2So Ezra the priest brought the law before the assembly which included men and women and all those able to understand what they heard. (This happened on the first day of the seventh month.) 3So he read it before the plaza in front of the Water Gate from dawn till noon before the men and women and those children who could understand. All the people were eager to hear the book of the law.

4Ezra the scribe stood on a towering wooden platform constructed for this purpose. Standing near him on his right were Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Masseiah. On his left were Pedaiah, Mishael, Malkijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam. 5Ezra opened the book in plain view of all the people, for he was elevated above all the people. When he opened the book, all the people stood up. 6Ezra blessed the [[sc:Lord]], the great God, and all the people replied “Amen! Amen!” as they lifted their hands. Then they bowed down and worshiped the [[sc:Lord]] with their faces to the ground.

7Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, and Pelaiah—all of whom were Levites —were teaching the people the law, as the people remained standing. 8They read from the book of God’s law, explaining it and imparting insight. Thus the people gained understanding from what was read.

9Then Nehemiah the governor, Ezra the priestly scribe, and the Levites who were imparting understanding to the people said to all of them, “This day is holy to the [[sc:Lord]] your God. Do not mourn or weep.” For all the people had been weeping when they heard the words of the law. 10He said to them, “Go and eat delicacies and drink sweet drinks and send portions to those for whom nothing is prepared. For this day is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the [[sc:Lord]] is your strength.”

11Then the Levites quieted all the people saying, “Be quiet, for this day is holy. Do not grieve.” 12So all the people departed to eat and drink and to share their food with others and to enjoy tremendous joy, for they had gained insight in the matters that had been made known to them.

13On the second day of the month the family leaders met with Ezra the scribe, together with all the people, the priests, and the Levites, to consider the words of the law. 14They discovered written in the law that the [[sc:Lord]] had commanded through Moses that the Israelites should live in temporary shelters during the festival of the seventh month, 15and that they should make a proclamation and disseminate this message in all their cities and in Jerusalem: “Go to the hill country and bring back olive branches and branches of wild olive trees, myrtle trees, date palms, and other leafy trees to construct temporary shelters, as it is written.”

16So the people went out and brought these things back and constructed temporary shelters for themselves, each on his roof and in his courtyard and in the courtyards of the temple of God and in the plaza of the Water Gate and the plaza of the Ephraim Gate. 17So all the assembly which had returned from the exile constructed temporary shelters and lived in them. The Israelites had not done so from the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day. Everyone experienced very great joy. 18Ezra read in the book of the law of God day by day, from the first day to the last. They observed the festival for seven days, and on the eighth day they held an assembly as was required.

Malachi 3:1–6 (NET)

1“I am about to send my messenger, who will clear the way before me. Indeed, the Lord you are seeking will suddenly come to his temple, and the messenger of the covenant, whom you long for, is certainly coming,” says the [[sc:Lord]] of Heaven’s Armies.

2Who can endure the day of his coming? Who can keep standing when he appears? For he will be like a refiner’s fire, like a launderer’s soap. 3He will act like a refiner and purifier of silver and will cleanse the Levites and refine them like gold and silver. Then they will offer the [[sc:Lord]] a proper offering. 4The offerings of Judah and Jerusalem will be pleasing to the [[sc:Lord]] as in former times and years past.

5“I will come to you in judgment. I will be quick to testify against those who practice divination; those who commit adultery; those who break promises; and those who exploit workers, widows, and orphans, who refuse to help the resident foreigner and in this way show they do not fear me,” says the [[sc:Lord]] of Heaven’s Armies.

6“Since, I, the [[sc:Lord]], do not go back on my promises, you, sons of Jacob, have not perished.

elements.text: A kingdom that will not end

elements.passageText:
9“While I was watching, thrones were set up, and the Ancient of Days took his seat. His attire was white like snow; the hair of his head was like lamb’s wool. His throne was ablaze with fire and its wheels were all aflame. 10A river of fire was streaming forth and proceeding from his presence. Many thousands were ministering to him; many tens of thousands stood ready to serve him. The court convened and the books were opened.

11“Then I kept on watching because of the arrogant words of the horn that was speaking. I was watching until the beast was killed and its body destroyed and thrown into the flaming fire. 12As for the rest of the beasts, their ruling authority had already been removed, though they were permitted to go on living for a time and a season.

13“I was watching in the night visions, And with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man was approaching. He went up to the Ancient of Days and was escorted before him. 14To him was given ruling authority, honor, and sovereignty. All peoples, nations, and language groups were serving him. His authority is eternal and will not pass away. His kingdom will not be destroyed.

elements.question: How is God described in verses 9–10, and what happens to the beast in verse 11?
elements.questionHint: Notice the throne, the books and the court.
elements.sampleAnswer: God is pictured as an ancient king in a court of law. He sits on a fiery throne, with snowy white clothing, surrounded by vast numbers of attendants. Records are opened and judgement begins. The terrifying beast is put to death and its body burned, showing that God is the true ruler who deals with the powers that stand against him.
elements.mainPoint: God is **the true King and Judge**, who destroys the powers that oppose him.

elements.question: Who comes before the Ancient of Days in verses 13–14, and what is he given?
elements.questionHint: Notice the words ‘all’ and ‘eternal’.
elements.sampleAnswer: A figure who looks human arrives in the clouds and is brought into God’s presence. He receives full governing power, glory and a kingdom. People of every race and tongue become his subjects. This rule is permanent: it will never pass away or be destroyed.
elements.mainPoint: God gives **an everlasting kingdom to one like a son of man**, over all peoples.

elements.text: A new creation

elements.passageText:
17For look, I am ready to create new heavens and a new earth! The former ones will not be remembered; no one will think about them anymore. 18But be happy and rejoice forevermore over what I am about to create! For look, I am ready to create Jerusalem to be a source of joy, and her people to be a source of happiness. 19Jerusalem will bring me joy, and my people will bring me happiness. The sound of weeping or cries of sorrow will never be heard in her again.

20Never again will one of her infants live just a few days or an old man die before his time. Indeed, no one will die before the age of one hundred; anyone who fails to reach the age of one hundred will be considered cursed. 21They will build houses and live in them; they will plant vineyards and eat their fruit. 22No longer will they build a house only to have another live in it, or plant a vineyard only to have another eat its fruit, for my people will live as long as trees, and my chosen ones will enjoy to the fullest what they have produced. 23They will not work in vain, or give birth to children that will experience disaster. For the [[sc:Lord]] will bless their children and their descendants. 24Before they even call out, I will respond; while they are still speaking, I will hear. 25A wolf and a lamb will graze together; a lion, like an ox, will eat straw, and a snake’s food will be dirt. They will no longer injure or destroy on my entire royal mountain,” says the [[sc:Lord]].

elements.question: What does God say he will create in verses 17–19, and how are people to respond?
elements.questionHint: Look at the first words of verse 17 and the verbs in verses 18 and 19.
elements.sampleAnswer: God announces a fresh start for the whole cosmos: he is about to create a new heaven and earth, so that the old order fades from memory. His people are urged to be glad and celebrate for ever what he makes. Jerusalem herself becomes a cause of delight, and the weeping and cries of distress that fill the present world will no more be heard there.
elements.mainPoint: God will **create a new heaven and earth**, with Jerusalem a joy and no more weeping.

elements.question: What will ordinary life look like in this new creation (verses 20–23)?
elements.questionHint: Think about homes, work, children and age.
elements.sampleAnswer: Life will be long and safe: babies will no longer die at birth, and no one will be cut off before reaching a ripe old age. People will construct homes and actually live in them, and plant vineyards and enjoy the harvest. Their labour will be fruitful, and their children will not face calamity. Ordinary things like housing, work and family are restored to what God intended.
elements.mainPoint: In the new creation **ordinary life is restored**: homes, work, family, long life and security.

elements.question: What happens to the animals in verse 25, and what is said about God’s mountain?
elements.questionHint: Look at the wolf and the lamb, and at the last words of the verse.
elements.sampleAnswer: Natural enemies will be at peace: lambs feed side by side with wolves, and lions eat straw like cattle. The snake is reduced to eating dirt. Nobody will injure or destroy anyone on God’s royal mountain, so it is a place of total safety. Creation as a whole is restored to harmony.
elements.mainPoint: God’s new creation brings **peace even to nature**, and safety on his mountain.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Compare the snake in verse 25 with the serpent in Genesis 3 (session 2). What do you notice?

elements.text: Putting it together

elements.question: What do these two passages promise that Israel still lacked while it was waiting? Think about king, people and place.
elements.questionHint: Think about who rules, who belongs and where they live.
elements.sampleAnswer: Daniel promises a ruler whose authority lasts for ever and covers all peoples. That answers the lack of a king. Isaiah promises new heavens and a new earth, with Jerusalem made new. That answers the lack of a place. Both include people from every nation under God’s rule, and they go beyond a return to Eden to a creation made new.
elements.mainPoint: The Old Testament ends with promises still waiting to be kept: **God’s people** from every nation, **God’s place** in a new creation, and **God’s rule** through an everlasting king.

elements.text: Reflect

elements.question: While Israel waited, God’s promises seemed unfulfilled. Which of God’s promises do you find it hardest to keep waiting for?

Isaiah’s picture of the new creation includes ordinary things: homes, gardens, work and children. What does that tell you about what God wants for the world? How might it change what you look forward to?

elements.text:
The Old Testament ends with a question: when will the promises come true? A king for ever, a servant who bears sin, a Son of Man given an everlasting kingdom, a covenant written on the heart and a new creation: all point forward to someone and something still to come. The New Testament study shows how the story continues.

Now tap Read more below to go deeper, and see the timeline of the whole Bible.

studyOnboardingSlides.heading: One story in eight passages
studyOnboardingSlides.body: This study traces the Old Testament’s story in eight key passages, from Eden to the hope of a new creation. Along the way you will see how God’s people, God’s place and God’s rule are lost, promised and partly restored.

The stretches of the story between the passages are summarised at the start of each session, so that you can follow the whole sweep even if you have not read it all.

The check works offline and never marks you. After you have answered, you can also look at the main point and a sample answer.
