sections.heading: About the Bible text and the other study

blocks.title: The Bible text
blocks.body: Passages are from the NET Bible. Under each passage, the link to NET takes you to netbible.org, where you can read the verses around it.

blocks.title: Part 1 of 2
blocks.body: This is the first of two studies. It takes the story from Eden to the hope of a new creation. The companion study, The Story of the Bible: New Testament, continues the story from the birth of Jesus.

body: These pages go further than the session. Each one fills in the part of the story that the session passes over, adds some background, and shows how the passage connects to the rest of the Bible.
Work through the session first, then tap Read more at its end to read the matching chapter here. The last chapter is a timeline of the whole Bible.

chapters.title: Eden and the shape of the story

footnotes.body: Christians who take the Bible as God’s Word read the ‘days’ of Genesis 1 in different ways, and differ over the age of the earth. This study does not depend on any one view. It asks what the passage says about God, humanity and the world.

before.body:
The session begins at Genesis 1:26, the sixth day. Before that, Genesis 1:1–25 describes God making light, sky, land and sea, plants, the sun, moon and stars, and the creatures that fill them.[[fn:1]] Most stages end with God’s verdict that it is good. The world is God’s own work: he speaks and it is. Nothing in it is a rival god, and nothing is an accident.

Genesis 1 builds towards humanity as its high point. Only humans are said to be made in God’s image. In the ancient world kings often set up statues of themselves to show their authority over a region. In the Bible, God sets up living images, men and women, to represent his rule in the world he has made.

garden.body:
Genesis 2 looks again at the sixth day from a closer angle. It is about the garden in Eden (the NET translates the Hebrew word as ‘orchard’; this study uses the more familiar ‘garden’) and the relationship between God and the first man and woman. The garden is more than a pleasant park. It is the place God has prepared for people to live, and the man is to ‘work’ it and ‘care for’ it. In Hebrew those two words are used together later for the duties of the Levites at the tent of meeting (Numbers 3:7–8). Many readers therefore see Eden as the first sanctuary, the place where God and people are meant to meet.

The two trees matter too. The tree of life stands for the life God gives. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil stands for the right to decide for oneself what is good, a right that belongs to God alone. Eden is a world of gift, with one boundary.

pattern.body:
Part of the kingdomIn EdenWhat to watch for
God’s peopleHumans made in God’s image, male and femaleHow a people for God is formed and grows
God’s placeThe garden in Eden, a home with God’s blessingThe land, Jerusalem and the new creation
God’s ruleGod’s word, and humans ruling under himThe law, the kings and the final King

psalm.body:
Psalm 8 is a short song that looks up at the night sky and asks why God should take any notice of human beings. Its answer echoes Genesis 1: God has crowned people with glory and honour, and has put the works of his hands under their feet. If you have time, read it beside Genesis 1:26–28. It shows that Israel’s own poets read Genesis as a statement of human dignity, which was never meant to make people proud, because the glory is a gift and the rule is shared out by God.

Notice, too, how the psalm begins and ends by praising God’s name. People are great because God has made them so, not because of anything they have achieved.

thread.body: As you move through the Old Testament, ask three questions of every episode. Who are God’s people here? Where are they? Who is ruling? The story keeps returning to these three things, and by the end each has been renewed.

footnotes.body: See Revelation 12:9, which speaks of ‘the ancient serpent, the one called the devil and Satan’.

meaning.body:
Genesis 3 explains what the rest of the Bible takes for granted: the world is not as it should be, and neither are we. It does not tell us where evil came from. It tells us how evil entered the human story, through a voice that contradicts what God has said, and through people who choose to listen to that voice rather than to God.

Notice how the temptation works. The serpent never says ‘rebel’. He makes God’s generous word sound like a restriction and suggests that God cannot be trusted. Sin begins as distrust, and distrust leads to a grab for independence.

serpent.body: Genesis says only that the serpent was more shrewd than the other creatures. Later Scripture identifies the enemy behind the serpent as the devil.[[fn:1]] The Bible does not offer a full account of where evil came from. What it gives is a clear verdict on how serious evil is, and a promise that it will be defeated.

broken.body:
RelationshipWhat Genesis 3 showsWhere the story points
With GodHiding, fear, and exile from the garden (3:8–10, 23–24)God’s law written on hearts and sins forgiven (Jeremiah 31:33–34)
With one anotherShame and blame (3:7, 12)A people who know God from the least to the greatest (Jeremiah 31:34)
With creationCursed ground and painful work (3:17–19)A new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17–25)

common.body:
Was it an apple? Genesis only says ‘fruit’. The apple comes from later tradition, probably because the Latin words for ‘apple’ and ‘evil’ sound alike. The passage tells us nothing about the kind of fruit, and the point is not the fruit but the command.

Why was the tree there at all? Genesis does not say. What it shows is a generous provision with one boundary: the tree gave the man and woman a daily chance to trust God’s word and to accept that he alone decides what is good.

Did they die that day? They did not drop dead, yet death came into their experience. They were shut out from the tree of life, God told them they would return to dust, and Paul later writes that death entered the world through one man (Romans 5:12). The loss of life began when the relationship with God was broken.

thread.body: Genesis 3:15 is often called the first gospel promise, because it is the first hint that God will rescue. The thread of the offspring begins here. In Genesis the line of the woman runs on through Seth and Noah to Abraham. Each time a child is born, the reader is invited to wonder whether this is the one. The story is moving slowly, but it is moving towards someone.

footnotes.body: ‘Abram’ means ‘exalted father’. In Genesis 17:5 God renames him ‘Abraham’, explained as ‘father of a multitude of nations’. Sarai is renamed Sarah.

before.body:
The first eleven chapters of Genesis show a repeating pattern: sin, judgement and grace. Cain kills Abel, and God protects Cain even while sending him away. Violence fills the earth, God judges it with the flood, and God saves Noah. After the flood God makes a covenant with Noah and all living creatures, and promises not to destroy the earth by flood again. Yet God notes that the human heart is still bent towards evil. At Babel people try to climb to the heavens to make a name for themselves, and God scatters them.

The pattern shows that judgement alone cannot fix the problem, because the problem is in people’s hearts. Genesis 12 is God’s answer. Instead of starting again, he starts a new line, and promises through it to bless the nations that Babel scattered.

abraham.body:
Genesis 12 and 15 introduce Abram, the man God would rename Abraham.[[fn:1]] Genesis 17 adds circumcision as the sign of the covenant. Abraham is not a perfect hero. He and Sarah try to bring about the promised child through Hagar (Genesis 16), and he twice passes Sarah off as his sister. The Bible does not hide the faults of its heroes, which makes plain that the promise depends on God, not on Abraham’s character.

The covenant was a long wait. Isaac, the promised son, was born when Abraham was a hundred. In Genesis 22 God tests Abraham by asking him to give up Isaac, and provides a substitute. The promise then passes down to Isaac, Jacob and Jacob’s twelve sons, including Joseph.

faith.body:
The New Testament returns to Abraham often. Paul quotes Genesis 15:6 to show that Abraham was counted righteous when he believed (Romans 4:3), and he says that the scripture ‘proclaimed the gospel to Abraham ahead of time’, with the promise that all the nations would be blessed in him (Galatians 3:8). The letter to the Hebrews points to the same man as an example of faith: he obeyed when called to go out, lived in tents in the promised land, and was looking forward to ‘the city with firm foundations, whose architect and builder is God’ (Hebrews 11:8–10).

These verses show what to watch for in the Old Testament story. The promise to Abraham is about far more than one family and one piece of land. It is the first stage of God’s plan to bless the world.

thread.body: Notice that the promise has three parts, matching the pattern: descendants (people), land (place) and blessing (a restored relationship with God, which is to reach the nations). The third part is the one we most easily forget. Abraham is not chosen instead of the nations but for their sake. The rest of the Old Testament keeps this in view, even when Israel forgets it. Isaiah later says that God’s servant is to be ‘a light to the nations’ (Isaiah 49:6).

footnotes.body: Christian traditions divide the commandments slightly differently, for example in how they count the first two. The content is the same.

rescue.body:
The book of Exodus has two halves. In chapters 1–18 God rescues Israel from Egypt. In chapters 19–40 he makes them his covenant people at Sinai and comes to live among them. The Passover is the pattern of rescue: the blood of a lamb marks each home and God’s judgement passes over. The Bible comes back to it again and again.

Exodus also records Israel’s complaints in the wilderness, and, while Moses is still on the mountain, the sin of the golden calf (Exodus 32). The people have been God’s own people for only weeks, and they already turn away. The story does not hide how easily the rescued people go astray.

law.body:
The Ten Commandments[[fn:1]] are the heart of a much larger body of law, found in the rest of Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. That law covers worship and sacrifice, justice and everyday life. Alongside it God gives the tabernacle, a tent where he will live among his people. The sacrifices make provision for sinful people to live near a holy God.

The law is given to people who have already been rescued. It tells them how to live as God’s people in God’s presence. Deuteronomy, Moses’ farewell sermons, sets out the choice before them: blessing for obedience, and exile for persistent disobedience. We shall meet those words again when the exile comes.

sealing.body:
After the Ten Commandments and the laws that follow them, Exodus 24 describes how the covenant was sealed. Moses reads the words aloud, and the people answer together that they are willing to do all that the Lord has said (24:3, 7). Moses then builds an altar, young men offer sacrifices, and he splashes half of the blood on the altar and half on the people, saying, ‘This is the blood of the covenant’ (24:8).

Two things stand out. The people promise obedience, and the story soon shows how fragile that promise is: before Moses has even come down from the mountain, they have made the golden calf (Exodus 32). And the covenant is sealed with blood, so that from the start the relationship between God and his people involves a death. Later sessions return to both of these.

thread.body: Israel’s calling to be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation shows what God’s kingdom is for. A priest brings people to God and God to people. Israel is set apart for God, in the middle of a world that belongs to God, so that the world may come to know him. Keep asking through the rest of the Old Testament whether Israel is living up to that calling.

footnotes.body: The ark of the covenant was the sacred chest that symbolised God’s presence with Israel. It was kept in the tabernacle, the tent God had told Moses to build, until the temple replaced it.

landfall.body:
The book of Joshua tells how Israel entered and took hold of the land. Judges then shows a cycle that repeats: the people turn from God, enemies oppress them, they cry out, and God sends a rescuer. By the end of the book the refrain is that there was no king in Israel. The story is asking for a king.

1 Samuel records the response. Israel demands a king ‘like the nations’, which shows how far they have drifted from trusting God as king. Saul looks the part but disobeys. David is a man after God’s own heart, though he too falls badly, as the story of Bathsheba shows (2 Samuel 11). Even so, under David the nation reaches its high point. He captures Jerusalem and brings the ark[[fn:1]] into the city.

promise.body:
The wordplay in 2 Samuel 7 is deliberate. David wants to build God a house (a temple). God replies that he will build David a house (a dynasty). The one who builds is the one who gives. God is not looking for builders. He is the builder.

The promise is picked up through the Old Testament. Psalm 2 and Psalm 72 picture the anointed king ruling to the ends of the earth. Psalm 89 recalls the promise and then laments that the king’s crown lies in the dust. The prophets look ahead to a king from David’s line who will rule with justice (Isaiah 9:6–7; 11:1–10; Jeremiah 23:5–6). Hope for a coming king is one of the strongest threads in the Old Testament.

afterdavid.body:
David’s son Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem, and when it was finished the glory of the Lord filled it (1 Kings 8:10–11). It looked as if the promise to David was being kept. But Solomon’s later years went badly, and after his death the kingdom split. Most of the tribes told Solomon’s son Rehoboam that they had no share in David and went home. From then on, only the tribe of Judah remained loyal to David’s dynasty (1 Kings 12:16–20).

David’s line continued to rule in Jerusalem for about four centuries, but most of its kings failed, and the promise of a king who would rule for ever seemed to be fading. That is why the prophets, whom we meet in the next sessions, keep returning to the hope of a king from David’s line who would do what the others had not.

thread.body: Notice how the covenants build on one another. The promise to Abraham gave a people, a land and blessing for the nations. The covenant at Sinai made the people a holy nation under God’s law. The promise to David adds the king through whom God will rule his people. Each step brings the kingdom nearer to its Eden pattern, and each step leaves something unfinished.

footnotes.body: Jerusalem fell in 586 BC; some scholars date the fall to 587 BC. The difference does not affect the story.

exile.body:
The exile was not a surprise. Moses had warned Israel at the end of Deuteronomy that unfaithfulness would end in exile. The prophets repeated the warning for centuries. The northern kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC, and Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 586 BC.[[fn:1]]

The exile was a disaster for the whole kingdom pattern. The people were scattered. The place was lost, because the land and the temple were taken. Even the king was gone: the last king of David’s line was taken captive. For a people who had believed God’s promises, it raised a painful question. Had God’s word failed?

hope.body:
The same prophets who warned of judgement also promised restoration. Jeremiah 30–33, often called the ‘book of consolation’, is full of hope for a people who have lost everything. The new covenant is its centre. Ezekiel, who was himself in exile, speaks in a similar way of God giving his people a new heart and putting his Spirit within them (Ezekiel 36:24–28).

Notice what is promised. It is not just a return to the land, but a deeper change. Exile showed that Israel could not keep the covenant, even in a good land and with a good law. Something would need to change in the people themselves.

covenants.body:
Covenant and passageWhat God promisesSign or seal
Noah (Genesis 9:8–17)Never again to destroy the earth by floodThe rainbow
Abraham (Genesis 15; 17)A people, a land and blessing for all nationsThe covenant ceremony; circumcision
Sinai (Exodus 19–24)Israel will be God’s treasured people, a kingdom of priests and a holy nationThe law; the Sabbath
David (2 Samuel 7)A son on David’s throne for everGod’s sworn promise (Psalm 89:3–4)
New (Jeremiah 31:31–34)The law on the heart, all knowing God, sins forgivenSeen fully in the New Testament study

jeremiah.body:
Jeremiah was called while he was young and protested that he did not know how to speak (Jeremiah 1:6). He spent decades warning Judah that Babylon would come, and he was mocked and persecuted for it. When his words were written on a scroll and read to the king, the king cut the scroll up and threw it on the fire (Jeremiah 36:23). Yet the words were written again, and they came true.

After the first exiles were taken to Babylon, Jeremiah wrote them a letter. They were to build houses, plant gardens, raise families and work for the peace of the city where God had sent them, praying to the Lord for it (Jeremiah 29:5–7). The new covenant promise belongs to the same hopeful message: God had not abandoned his people, and the exile would not be the end.

thread.body: Each covenant adds to the one before. None replaces the promise to Abraham: the later covenants unfold it. The new covenant promises what the others had left unfinished, which is a people who can keep faith with God because he has changed them.

footnotes.body: The Hebrew word is often translated ‘guilt offering’ or ‘restitution offering’. See Leviticus 5:14–6:7 for the sacrifice it names.

setting.body:
The book of Isaiah moves from warnings of judgement to words of comfort to a vision of a new creation. Its central chapters (40–55) speak comfort to a people facing exile and promise that God will bring them home, and that he will do so in a way that surprises them. The servant is the key to that surprise.

When the exiles did return, under Cyrus of Persia, many found it disappointing. The temple was a shadow of Solomon’s. They were still under foreign rule. The question was whether the great promises of Isaiah had been kept. The book of Isaiah suggested that something more was needed.

songs.header: The four songs of the servant
songs.body:
Isaiah 52:13–53:12 is the fourth of four ‘songs of the servant’ (42:1–9; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12). In the first the servant brings justice to the nations. In the second he is called ‘Israel’ yet has a mission to restore Israel, and to be a light to the nations. In the third he is obedient and endures abuse. In the fourth he suffers and dies, and is raised to honour.

The identity of the servant puzzled readers long before the New Testament. Isaiah uses ‘servant’ for the whole nation, and also for one who rescues the nation. Sometimes the servant is Israel, and sometimes he stands apart from Israel to restore it. The New Testament study shows how that puzzle is resolved.

quoted.body:
The New Testament quotes this song often. Jesus says that the words ‘he was counted with the transgressors’ must be fulfilled in him (Luke 22:37). In Acts 8 an Ethiopian official is reading about the sheep led to slaughter and asks Philip who the prophet is talking about, and Philip begins with that passage and tells him the good news about Jesus (Acts 8:32–35). Peter, writing to suffering Christians, says that Jesus bore our sins in his body on the tree, and that by his wounds we were healed (1 Peter 2:24).

You do not need to read these now. But they show how early Christians understood the song, and they prepare the way for the New Testament study.

thread.body: The sacrifices of Leviticus taught that sin cost a life, and that God provided an animal in the sinner’s place.[[fn:1]] Isaiah 53 goes further. The servant is the one who is wounded for others’ rebellion, and the passage speaks of a human life as the offering. Keep this in view as we turn to the New Testament study, where the cross is central.

footnotes.body: The Hebrew Bible places its books in a different order from English Bibles, and ends with 2 Chronicles. The last words of 2 Chronicles (36:22–23) invite the exiles to go up to Jerusalem.

waiting.body:
After the return, the Old Testament’s storyline gradually fades. Haggai and Zechariah urged the rebuilding of the temple. Ezra and Nehemiah led spiritual and civil renewal. Malachi, the last prophet, promised that God would send a messenger to prepare the way and would himself come to his temple. Then prophetic speech stops.

In the centuries that followed, Persia gave way to Greece, and Greece to Rome. Faithful Jews gathered around the Scriptures in local synagogues, and many looked for the day when God would keep his promises. It was a time of intense hope and of great frustration.

daniel.body:
Daniel 7 is a vision. Four beasts rise from the sea, standing for empires that dominate the world. Then the scene changes to the throne room of heaven, where God, the Ancient of Days, takes his seat and the beasts lose their power. The kingdom is given to ‘one like a son of man’, a human figure who comes with the clouds and receives everlasting rule over all peoples.

The vision is full of symbols and is not meant to be decoded detail by detail. The main point is that the nations’ rulers are not the last word. God is on the throne, and he gives the kingdom to a figure who is human and who also approaches God in a way no ordinary person would. The phrase ‘son of man’ matters later in the story.

visions.body:
Daniel 7 begins with four great beasts rising out of the sea. When Daniel asks what the vision means, he is told that the beasts stand for four kings, and then comes the surprising point: ‘the holy ones of the Most High will receive the kingdom’ and possess it for ever (Daniel 7:15–18). Later the angel adds that the kingdom, authority and greatness of all the kingdoms under heaven will be given to ‘the people of the holy ones of the Most High’, and that all authorities will serve him and obey him (7:27).

So the vision describes both a single figure, one like a son of man, and a people who share his kingdom. This pairing of a ruler and his people fits the pattern of the whole Bible story. It will matter in the New Testament study, which shows how Jesus describes himself as the Son of Man.

thread.body: The Hebrew Bible ends with an invitation to ‘go up’ to Jerusalem,[[fn:1]] and the English Old Testament ends with a promise of a messenger. Either way, the story is left open. Eight passages have given us the shape of the story: a kingdom made, lost, promised, partly known, broken and promised again. Everything now depends on whether God keeps his word.

footnotes.body: Evangelical scholars differ over the date of the exodus, arguing for both an earlier date (about 1446 BC) and a later one (about 1260 BC). Nothing in this study depends on the choice.

about.body: The Bible’s story runs across many centuries. This chart places the eight passages of this study (marked with their session numbers) in the whole sweep, and looks ahead to the New Testament. Dates are approximate. Genesis 1–11 gives no dates, so none are suggested for the period before Abraham.

leadersNotesData.subtitle: Notes for group leaders
intro: These studies are written for groups of about six to ten, and work for individuals too. Each session is planned for about 90 minutes; the notes suggest a shorter route if you have 60.

Aim to let the group find answers in the passage rather than hearing them from you. The sample answers show what the text contains; they are not a script, and a good answer may be put quite differently.

Each session’s notes give the aim, suggested timing, how to lead it, what to watch for, tricky points, and how the session fits the big story. The Go Deeper chapters give background you can use if the group asks for more.

aim.body: To help the group see that the Bible is one story, and that Eden sets out the pattern of people, place and rule which the rest of the story follows.

timing.body: Welcome and opening question, 10 minutes. Genesis 1:26–2:3, 20 minutes. Genesis 2:4–25, 30 minutes. Summary question, 10 minutes. Reflection, 15 minutes. Prayer, 5 minutes. For 60 minutes: skip the opening question and the ‘Go deeper’ question, and discuss only one reflection question.

lead.body: This session sets the habits for the course: read the passage aloud, ask for answers from the text, and keep the big picture in view. Write ‘people, place, rule’ where everyone can see it, and bring it back each week. Show anyone new to the app how to open a passage by tapping its reference.

watch.body: Members who want to debate how God made the world. Gently steer back to what the passage says about who God is, who we are and what the world is for.

tricky.body: Genesis 1–2 are read in different ways, even among those who hold the Bible’s full authority, including the length of the ‘days’ and the age of the earth. The session does not depend on any of these. If someone asks about ‘Let us make’ in 1:26, say that the Bible shows more of who God is as the story goes on.

thread.body: Everything in the course is measured against this picture: God’s people, in God’s place, under God’s rule.

aim.body: To see what sin is (distrust of God’s word that breaks every relationship) and to catch the first hint of rescue in 3:15.

timing.body: Opening question, 10 minutes. Questions on the passage, 50 minutes. Reflection, 20 minutes. Prayer, 10 minutes. For 60 minutes: use the opening question as a brief icebreaker and take only one reflection question.

lead.body: Read the whole chapter aloud, perhaps with different voices for the narrator, the serpent, the woman and God. Ask the group what the serpent does with God’s words, before looking at the consequences.

watch.body: Members who want to spend the whole time on who the serpent is, or on blaming Eve. Keep the focus on the pattern: doubt, grasp, hide, blame. Also watch for a rush to explain 3:15 in full New Testament terms. Let the group say what the verse itself says: a promised offspring who defeats the serpent at a cost.

tricky.body: Genesis 3:16 is read in different ways, and some groups will want to debate marriage roles. Say that the verse describes how sin damages the relationship, and move on. The angelic sentries and the whirling sword need not be pressed for detail.

thread.body: Everything lost here (people, place and rule) is what the rest of the story promises to restore. Verse 15 is the first seed of that promise.

aim.body: To see that God’s answer to a fallen world is a promise, which Abram receives by faith, and that the promise is for the whole world.

timing.body: Opening question, 10 minutes. Genesis 12:1–9, 20 minutes. Genesis 15, 30 minutes. Summary question, 10 minutes. Reflection, 15 minutes. Prayer, 5 minutes. For 60 minutes: skip the opening question and the summary question.

lead.body: Spend a few minutes retelling Genesis 4–11 using the bridge text, so that those who have not read it can follow. Then let the group find the promises in 12:1–3 for themselves. Ask them what Abram has to go on.

watch.body: Members who talk about Abram’s faith as something he earned. Genesis 15:6 says the Lord counted it as righteousness: the emphasis is on the God who promises.

tricky.body: The covenant ceremony in chapter 15 is strange to modern readers. Do not over-explain it. The main point is that God binds himself to keep his promise. Someone may ask about the modern state of Israel when you reach the land promise. Stay with what this passage says. The land promise keeps developing across the story, and the New Testament study returns to it.

thread.body: The promise has three parts (descendants, land and blessing) that match people, place and rule. The blessing for all nations is the part to keep in view.

aim.body: To see that God rescues first and gives his law to a rescued people, and that Israel’s calling was a gift with a purpose.

timing.body: Opening question, 10 minutes. Exodus 19:1–8, 20 minutes. Exodus 20:1–17, 35 minutes. Reflection, 15 minutes. Prayer, 10 minutes. For 60 minutes: take the opening question briefly and look at only two of the three Exodus 20 questions.

lead.body: Spend a few minutes on the bridge text, since many group members will know the Exodus story in pieces. Draw out the order: rescue (19:4), relationship (19:5–6), then rules (20:1–17). Invite each person to say which command they find most striking.

watch.body: The idea that the Old Testament is about earning God’s favour and the New Testament about grace. Sinai begins with grace. Also watch for a purely rule-keeping attitude in the discussion of the commands.

tricky.body: Members may ask how the law applies to Christians. Park it: say that the New Testament study returns to this, and keep this session on what the passage says. ‘Kingdom of priests’ is also often misread. Keep to what the text says: Israel set apart for God in a world that belongs to him.

thread.body: God’s people now have rescue and a rule. The place is still to come, and the story soon shows that the people themselves need changing.

aim.body: To see that God promises a king whose rule will last for ever, and that God himself is the builder of his kingdom.

timing.body: Opening question, 10 minutes. 2 Samuel 7:1–17, 40 minutes. David’s prayer, 15 minutes. Reflection, 15 minutes. Prayer, 10 minutes. For 60 minutes: take the opening question briefly and ask only the questions on verses 4–7 and 11–16, then one reflection.

lead.body: Ask someone to read the passage aloud, and listen for the word ‘house’ as it changes meaning. The questions follow the passage in order, so let the group notice who is speaking and who is acting.

watch.body: Members who rush to say that the promised son is Jesus. They may well be right, but ask them first what David himself would have understood. Let the question of ‘for ever’ stay open for now.

tricky.body: The promise says ‘for ever’, yet the Davidic kings ended in exile in 586 BC. This is the tension the passage deliberately creates, and it is resolved later in the story. The reference to the king doing wrong (7:14) is part of the promise: God will discipline, not abandon.

thread.body: The kingdom now has its three parts again: a people (Israel), a place (the land) and a king (David and his line). The promise of an everlasting king is waiting to be kept.

aim.body: To see that Israel’s problem went deeper than the law could reach, and that God promised to change his people from the inside and forgive their sin.

timing.body: Opening question, 10 minutes. Retell the bridge text, 10 minutes. Questions on Jeremiah 31:31–34, 40 minutes. Reflection, 20 minutes. Prayer, 10 minutes. For 60 minutes: shorten the bridge text and discuss only one reflection question.

lead.body: The passage is short, so read it slowly twice. Ask the group to underline every ‘I will’. Then use the covenants table in Go Deeper to show how this promise completes the earlier ones.

watch.body: Talk that makes the old covenant sound like a mistake. Verse 32 locates the failure in the people, not in God’s covenant.

tricky.body: Jeremiah says the covenant is made with ‘the people of Israel and Judah’. Some will ask who the new covenant people are. Say that the question is a good one and that the New Testament study returns to it. Do not let it take over the session.

thread.body: This is the hinge of the Old Testament’s hope: God will deal with the heart and with sin. The next session asks how that forgiveness can be given.

aim.body: To see that the Old Testament itself points to someone who will bear the sin of others, and to feel the weight of 53:4–6.

timing.body: Opening question, 10 minutes. The passage in five stages, 50 minutes. Reflection, 20 minutes. Prayer, 10 minutes. For 60 minutes: take the opening question briefly, combine the questions on 53:1–3 and 53:7–9, and take one reflection.

lead.body: Read the passage aloud slowly, perhaps with a different reader for each of the five stages. Notice the shift from ‘he’ to ‘we’ in 53:1 and 53:4–6, and ask who is speaking. Leave room for silence before the reflection.

watch.body: The group will probably name Jesus at once. That is fine, but ask them to say first what the passage itself says. Also watch for any softening of the words about punishment and bearing sin: the passage speaks plainly of the servant suffering in the place of others.

tricky.body: Questions about who wrote Isaiah are best left aside. Stay with the passage. The servant is not named, so it is fair to treat the identity as an open question for now. The New Testament study picks it up.

thread.body: The covenant promised forgiveness. The servant shows how: through one who bears sin. This is the Old Testament’s deepest anticipation of the cross.

aim.body: To see the hope with which the Old Testament closes, and to gather up the story so far: a King, a covenant, a servant and a new creation still to come.

timing.body: Opening question, 10 minutes. Daniel 7:9–14, 20 minutes. Isaiah 65:17–25, 30 minutes. Summary question, 10 minutes. Reflection, 15 minutes. Prayer, 5 minutes. For 60 minutes: skip the opening question and the ‘Go deeper’ question and take one reflection.

lead.body: This is a good session to review the whole course. Before the summary question, ask the group to recall one thing from each of the earlier sessions, and write the answers on a sheet under ‘people’, ‘place’ and ‘rule’. Then point them to the timeline in Go Deeper.

watch.body: Attempts to turn the visions into a timetable of future events. Both passages are poetic and symbolic. Keep to what they say about God’s rule, his people and his new creation.

tricky.body: Isaiah 65:20 is puzzling, since it speaks of death in a new creation. Treat it as a picture of life that is long, secure and blessed, and leave detailed explanations aside. The New Testament study looks at what the New Testament says about death in the new creation. Do not be drawn into debates about the order of end-time events; the next study stops at Revelation 21–22 on purpose.

thread.body: The Old Testament closes with all three parts of the kingdom promised and none finished. The New Testament study picks up the story with the arrival of the King.
